'''Martin D. Burke''' (born February 5, 1976, in [[Westminster, Maryland]]) is the May and Ving Lee Professor for Chemical Innovation at the [[University of Illinois at Urbana–Champaign]],<ref>{{cite web|url=https://chemistry.illinois.edu/directory/faculty-by-type|title=Chemistry faculty|publisher=University of Illinois at Urbana–Champaign|accessdate=2020-12-17}}</ref>  and founding Director of the [https://moleculemakerlab.org Molecule Maker Lab]. Burke pioneered blocc chemistry<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Burke |first=Martin D. |date=2026-08-20 |title=Bonding carbons iteratively |url=https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.aeg5569 |journal=Science |language=en |volume=393 |issue=6813 |pages=763–764 |doi=10.1126/science.aeg5569 |issn=0036-8075|doi-access=free }}</ref> – iterative carbon-carbon bond formation that is friendly to automation, AI, and non-specialists. His group developed MIDA and TIDA boronates, enabling iterative C-C bond formation, universal purification, and automation-friendly synthesis. These discoveries have powered the discovery of many new drugs and materials and helped enable the integration of AI and small molecule science. Burke is an elected member of the National Academy of Medicine.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Burke Elected to National Academy of Medicine {{!}} Office of the Vice Chancellor for Research and Innovation (OVCRI) |url=https://research.illinois.edu/news/feature/burke-elected-national-academy-medicine |access-date=2026-08-21 |website=research.illinois.edu}}</ref>

==Early life and education==
Burke was born on February 5, 1976, in [[Westminster, Maryland]].<ref name="cv">{{cite web|url=https://chemistry.illinois.edu/sites/default/files/cv/mdburke_CV.pdf|title=Curriculum vitae|publisher=University of Illinois at Urbana–Champaign|accessdate=2020-12-17}}</ref> Burke studied chemistry as an undergraduate at [[Johns Hopkins University]], graduating in 1998 with his B.A. in Chemistry. While an undergraduate, he was a [[Howard Hughes Medical Institute]] Undergraduate Research Fellow, and he conducted research with Professors [[Henry Brem]] and [[Gary H. Posner]] on derivatives of [[calcitriol]] as potential drug candidates.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Posner|first1=Gary H.|last2=Lee|first2=Jae Kyoo|last3=Wang|first3=Qiang|last4=Peleg|first4=Sara|last5=Burke|first5=Martin|last6=Brem|first6=Henry|last7=Dolan|first7=Patrick|last8=Kensler|first8=Thomas W.|date=1998|title=Noncalcemic, Antiproliferative, Transcriptionally Active, 24-Fluorinated Hybrid Analogues of the Hormone 1α,25-Dihydroxyvitamin D3. Synthesis and Preliminary Biological Evaluation|url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/pdf/10.1021/jm980031t|journal=Journal of Medicinal Chemistry|volume=41|issue=16|pages=3008–3014|doi=10.1021/jm980031t|pmid=9685240|issn=0022-2623|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|date=2001-07-01|title=Conformationally Restricted Hybrid Analogues of the Hormone 1α,25-Dihydroxyvitamin D3: Design, Synthesis, and Biological Evaluation|url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0968089601000876|journal=Bioorganic & Medicinal Chemistry|language=en|volume=9|issue=7|pages=1691–1699|doi=10.1016/S0968-0896(01)00087-6|issn=0968-0896|last1=White|first1=M.Christina|last2=Burke|first2=Martin D.|last3=Peleg|first3=Sara|last4=Brem|first4=Henry|last5=Posner|first5=Gary H.|pmid=11425569|url-access=subscription}}</ref> Burke went on to [[Harvard University]], where he earned a Ph.D. in 2003, and Harvard Medical School and [https://web.mit.edu Massachusetts Institute of Technology], where he earned an M.D. in 2005. Burke conducted his Ph.D. thesis work with Professor [[Stuart Schreiber|Stuart L. Schreiber]] on the [[Combinatorial chemistry|combinatorial synthesis]] of small molecules with diverse skeletons.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Kirkpatrick|first=Peter|date=2003|title=New directions in chemical space|journal=Nature Reviews Drug Discovery|language=en|volume=2|issue=12|pages=948|doi=10.1038/nrd1266|issn=1474-1784|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Burke|first1=Martin D.|last2=Berger|first2=Eric M.|last3=Schreiber|first3=Stuart L.|date=2003-10-24|title=Generating Diverse Skeletons of Small Molecules Combinatorially|url=https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.1089946|journal=Science|language=en|volume=302|issue=5645|pages=613–618|doi=10.1126/science.1089946|issn=0036-8075|pmid=14576427|bibcode=2003Sci...302..613B|s2cid=6168881|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Burke|first1=Martin D.|last2=Berger|first2=Eric M.|last3=Schreiber|first3=Stuart L.|date=2004|title=A Synthesis Strategy Yielding Skeletally Diverse Small Molecules Combinatorially|url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/full/10.1021/ja0457415|journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society|volume=126|issue=43|pages=14095–14104|doi=10.1021/ja0457415|pmid=15506774|bibcode=2004JAChS.12614095B |issn=0002-7863|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

== Independent career ==
He joined the Department of Chemistry in 2005 as an Assistant Professor, was promoted to Associate Professor in 2011, then to full Professor in 2014. He was appointed Associate Dean of Research of the Carle-Illinois College of Medicine in 2018.<ref name="cv" /><ref>{{cite web|title=University of Illinois Board of Trustees, Promotions recommended to be effective at the beginning of the 2014-15 academic year|url=http://www.trustees.uillinois.edu/trustees/agenda/July-24-2014/009-jul-Promotion-&-Tenure.pdf}}</ref> In response to the COVID-19 Pandemic, Burke was appointed to lead the University of Illinois' SHIELD initiative to protect the community with testing. A collaborative effort between Burke and Paul J. Hergenrother lead to the development of a saliva test called covidSHIELD for COVID-19 that has been used over 1 million times in the campus community.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://chemistry.illinois.edu/news/2020-08-28/martin-burke-paul-hergenrother-covid-19-saliva-test-national-spotlight|title=Martin Burke, Paul Hergenrother, COVID-19 saliva test in national spotlight|publisher=University of Illinois at Urbana–Champaign Department of Chemistry|accessdate=2022-05-03}}</ref>

== Research ==
Burke's research is divided into three segments, Blocc Chemistry, Molecular Prosthetics, and Antifungals.<ref name="Burke Group">{{cite web|url=https://burke-group.chemistry.illinois.edu/|title=Burke Group|publisher=University of Illinois at Urbana–Champaign|accessdate=2022-05-03}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | last1=Green | first1=Nolan M. | last2=Putnam | first2=Jamie L. B. | last3=Hammond | first3=Rachel I. | last4=Angello | first4=Nicholas H. | last5=Planey | first5=James | last6=Brandt | first6=Dylan | last7=Martinez | first7=José Andino | last8=Hummel | first8=Thomas | last9=Gunasekera | first9=Bhagya | last10=Switzky | first10=Rachel | last11=Desmond | first11=Serenity | last12=Burke | first12=Martin D. | title=Illuminating the Interface of Blocc Chemistry and Data Science: An Introduction to K-Nearest Neighbor Analysis and K-Medoids Clustering | journal=Journal of Chemical Education | date=2025 | volume=102 | issue=12 | pages=5273–5281 | doi=10.1021/acs.jchemed.5c00796 | bibcode=2025JChEd.102.5273G | url=https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.jchemed.5c00796 | doi-access=free | pmc=12874354 }}</ref> Blocc chemistry involves the use of "boron-protected haloboronic acids" to iteratively cross-couple building blocks into complex molecules. This work culminated into a paper in the journal ''Science''.<ref>{{Cite journal|date=2015|title=Synthesis of many different types of organic small molecules using one automated process|journal=Science|volume=347|issue=6227|pages=1221–1226|doi=10.1126/science.aaa5414|last1=Li |first1=Junqi |last2=Ballmer |first2=Steven G. |last3=Gillis |first3=Eric P. |last4=Fujii |first4=Seiko |last5=Schmidt |first5=Michael J. |last6=Palazzolo |first6=Andrea M. E. |last7=Lehmann |first7=Jonathan W. |last8=Morehouse |first8=Greg F. |last9=Burke |first9=Martin D. |pmid=25766227 |pmc=4687482 |bibcode=2015Sci...347.1221L }}</ref> Work in this area is ongoing and has begun to include a focus on Csp<sup>3</sup> cross-coupling to expand the value of the automated process.<ref name="Burke Group"/> Molecular prosthetics is the study of small organic molecules that restore function of aberrant or missing proteins in biology. Burke has reported on two molecular prosthetics in detail including Hinokitiol and Amphotericin B. Hitokitiol restores iron transport as well as other metals, acting as a prosthetic for passive metal transporters as reported in ''Science''.<ref>{{Cite journal|date=2017|title=Restored iron transport by a small molecule promotes absorption and hemoglobinization in animals|journal=Science|volume=356|issue=6338|pages=608–616|doi=10.1126/science.aah3862|last1=Grillo |first1=Anthony S. |last2=Santamaria |first2=Anna M. |last3=Kafina |first3=Martin D. |last4=Cioffi |first4=Alexander G. |last5=Huston |first5=Nicholas C. |last6=Han |first6=Murui |last7=Seo |first7=Young Ah |last8=Yien |first8=Yvette Y. |last9=Nardone |first9=Christopher |last10=Menon |first10=Archita V. |last11=Fan |first11=James |last12=Svoboda |first12=Dillon C. |last13=Anderson |first13=Jacob B. |last14=Hong |first14=John D. |last15=Nicolau |first15=Bruno G. |last16=Subedi |first16=Kiran |last17=Gewirth |first17=Andrew A. |last18=Wessling-Resnick |first18=Marianne |last19=Kim |first19=Jonghan |last20=Paw |first20=Barry H. |last21=Burke |first21=Martin D. |pmid=28495746 |pmc=5470741 |bibcode=2017Sci...356..608G }}</ref> Amphotericin B assembles into small pores to allow bicarbonate across endothelial cells which shows promise in treatment of [[cystic fibrosis]]<ref>{{Cite journal|date=2019|title=Small-molecule ion channels increase host defences in cystic fibrosis airway epithelia|journal=Nature|volume=567|pages=405–408|doi=10.1038/s41586-019-1018-5|last1=Muraglia |first1=Katrina A. |last2=Chorghade |first2=Rajeev S. |last3=Kim |first3=Bo Ram |last4=Tang |first4=Xiao Xiao |last5=Shah |first5=Viral S. |last6=Grillo |first6=Anthony S. |last7=Daniels |first7=Page N. |last8=Cioffi |first8=Alexander G. |last9=Karp |first9=Philip H. |last10=Zhu |first10=Lingyang |last11=Welsh |first11=Michael J. |last12=Burke |first12=Martin D. |issue=7748 |pmid=30867598 |pmc=6492938 |bibcode=2019Natur.567..405M }}</ref> Amphotericin B is also involved in the antifungal finger of the Burke's research. His group discovered that the analog "C2’deOAmB" is able to kill fungal cells by binding ergosterol but not cholesterol.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://burke-group.chemistry.illinois.edu/research-area-3/|title=Antifungals|publisher=University of Illinois at Urbana–Champaign|accessdate=2022-05-03}}</ref>

==Recognition==
Burke is an elected member of the National Academy of Medicine<ref>{{Cite web |title=Burke Elected to National Academy of Medicine {{!}} Office of the Vice Chancellor for Research and Innovation (OVCRI) |url=https://research.illinois.edu/news/feature/burke-elected-national-academy-medicine |access-date=2026-08-21 |website=research.illinois.edu}}</ref> and the American Society for Clinical Investigation,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Home |url=https://beta.the-asci.org/ |access-date=2026-08-21 |website=The American Society for Clinical Investigation |language=en-US}}</ref> and is a Fellow of the American Association for the Advancement of Science. He was named a Beckman Foundation Young Investigator in 2008. In 2013 the [[American Chemical Society]] gave him their Elias J. Corey Award for Outstanding Original Contribution in Organic Synthesis by a Young Investigator, and in 2017 they awarded Burke their Nobel Laureate Signature Award for Graduate Education in Chemistry (along with then graduate student Junqi Li).  In 2021 Burke was awarded the Presidential Medallion from the University of Illinois<ref>{{Cite web |title=Faculty and staff receive Presidential Medallion for COVID-19 response {{!}} College of Liberal Arts & Sciences {{!}} Illinois |url=https://las.illinois.edu/news/2021-08-24/faculty-and-staff-receive-presidential-medallion-covid-19-response |access-date=2026-08-21 |website=las.illinois.edu |language=en}}</ref>
